title: DevOps engineer

manager.name: Tess
manager.title: Engineering Manager
manager.persona_note: Tess is dealing with something that just went wrong. A good recruiter helps separate the urgent fix from the long-term job.

teaser: Tess's website crashed during exams last week. Tess needs help now.
context: The company runs online courses and has about 100 people.
The engineer keeps the website and servers running.
message: Hi, our site crashed during exam week, right when students needed it most. I need a DevOps engineer, and I need one fast.
The job ad was written in a hurry, so it may not be quite right.
Do you have ten minutes to go over what we need?
framing: Kickoff calls are often short, and hiring managers have a lot on their plate. Tess will share a few first thoughts about the role. Good questions help you both get it right.
end_early: Sorry, I've got to run. Send me what you've got.

needs.n1: Someone to make the website reliable before the next exam season.
needs.n2: Someone to build new features for students.

beats.label: The outage
beats.sam: We need someone now. Our site went down right in the middle of exam week.

choices.text: That sounds really stressful. What happened, and is it fixed for now?
choices.reply: It's patched. It broke because nobody had planned for that many students at once.
choices.why: Asking about the crisis first shows what the new hire really needs to prevent.

choices.text: Understood. Should I start today and send you whoever is available fastest?
choices.why: Speed helps, but you'd be hiring for this week's emergency rather than the job itself.

choices.text: Isn't rushing a hire after an outage how teams end up with more problems?
choices.reply: I don't have time for that.
choices.why: There's truth in it, but said this way it sounds like a lecture during a stressful week.

choices.text: What would need to be in place so it doesn't happen next exam season?
choices.reply: Testing the site under heavy load, and planning ahead for busy weeks.
choices.why: A follow-up on prevention turns a crisis into the real, long-term job.

choices.text: So is it mainly a question of adding more servers before the next busy season?
choices.why: A leading guess missed the real need and got a short answer.

choices.text: Why wasn't that planning done before exam week?
choices.reply: We had nobody to do it.
choices.why: It sounds like blame, and the manager closes up just when you need them to open up.

beats.label: On call
beats.sam: They'll be on call all the time.

choices.text: Constant on-call can make this hard to fill. Could it be shared across the team?
choices.reply: We could rotate it between three people, I suppose.
choices.why: Raising the risk gently, as a question, often leads to a more realistic and attractive job.

choices.text: How often does something actually break outside working hours?
choices.why: A good question, but you let 'all the time' stand, and candidates will notice.

choices.text: Should I tell candidates they'll be on call around the clock?
choices.why: Agreeing builds burnout into the job, which drives good people away.

beats.label: Every cloud
beats.sam: They must know every major cloud platform.

choices.text: Which cloud platforms does your team use today?
choices.why: Checking a must-have against the real setup often shows it isn't needed.

choices.text: Got it. Should I look for people with experience across all the major platforms?
choices.why: It narrows the search for no reason when the team only uses one platform.

choices.text: So the more platforms someone knows, the better?
choices.why: A leading question locked in a filter that doesn't fit the job.

beats.label: Start date
beats.sam: I'd like them to start within two weeks.

choices.text: I can work with that urgency. Would you be open to a short process so we can move quickly?
choices.why: Agreeing to the urgency, with a practical plan, builds trust and keeps things moving.

choices.text: Is two weeks a firm date, or is there some flexibility?
choices.why: It's a fair check, but it can sound like doubt during a stressful week.

choices.text: Most good engineers need to give notice. Isn't two weeks a bit unrealistic?
choices.why: There's truth in it, but pushing back makes the manager dig in on the date.

beats.label: The pay

choices.text: That's great to hear. What range is approved today, so I know where to aim?
choices.why: Even 'whatever it takes' has a number. Asking kindly gets it.

choices.text: That's helpful, but I'll need an actual range. What's been approved?
choices.why: It worked, but it cost goodwill. A friendly question gets the same answer.

choices.text: Wonderful. Shall I tell candidates pay is open?
choices.why: Without a range, you can't tell which candidates the manager can actually afford.

beats.note: Since January 2026, many Ontario employers must include the expected pay or a pay range in public job postings.

beats.label: Remote
beats.sam: Remote is completely fine for this role.

choices.text: That widens the search a lot. Can I lead with that when I reach out to people?
choices.why: A quick yes on a real perk gives you a strong selling point.

choices.text: Will there be any travel or in-person days at all?
choices.why: It's fair to ask, but it doesn't change the search much.

choices.text: Wouldn't having someone in the office help during the next outage?
choices.why: Pushing back on something that's already fine spends goodwill for nothing.

beats.label: The real job
beats.sam: Honestly, they'll just keep the servers running.

choices.text: Once things are stable, what would you want them to work on?
choices.reply: Preparing us to grow without crashing again.
choices.why: Asking about the long-term job finds the pitch, and it's far more appealing than firefighting.

choices.text: So should I describe it as a role keeping things stable?
choices.why: That makes the job sound like firefighting forever, which puts off strong engineers.

choices.text: Isn't there a lot more to the job than that?
choices.why: Questioning the manager's description rarely changes it. Asking about the future does.

candidates.name: Jordan
candidates.job: DevOps engineer at a ticket-selling site
facts: Prepared a site for huge sale days
Runs load tests before busy seasons
Shares on-call with a small team

reason.n1: Prepares busy sites for peak days and shares on-call. That's the long-term job Tess needs, inside the range.

view.n1: Jordan would keep exam week boring. In a good way.

candidates.name: Wren
candidates.job: Platform engineer at a software company
facts: Runs load tests before big launches
Works on a team without on-call duties

reason.n1: Strong on preparation, but hasn't done on-call. Even shared across three people, this job needs it.

view.n1: Wren is great, but someone has to answer when it breaks.

candidates.name: Neve
facts: Strong at setting up new systems

reason.n1: Knowing every cloud matches the old ad, but Tess uses one, and the job is long-term reliability, not short projects.

view.n1: Neve would be gone before exam season.

candidates.name: Rhys
candidates.job: Site reliability engineer at a famous streaming company
facts: Led the response to major outages
Known for fixing problems fast under pressure
Works with a team of 30 engineers

reason.n1: The most impressive record, but built on fixing outages, not preventing them. Tess said the job is testing and planning so it doesn't happen again.

view.n1: Rhys fixes fires. I need someone who prevents them.
